This is a step-by-step audio-guided walking tour of Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

Stop 1: Cathedral

Coordinates: 10.779722, 106.699167

Type/Specialty: Historic Landmark

Specific Examples: Stained glass windows, French colonial architecture, peaceful gardens

You stand before the Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica of Saigon, solemnly inaugurated on Easter, 11 April 1880, after three years of construction funded entirely by the French colonial government at a cost of 2,500,000 French francs. In 1903, the colonial government erected a bronze statue here in the garden, depicting French Catholic priest Pierre Pigneau de Béhaine alongside the juvenile Prince Nguyễn Phúc Cảnh, giving the square its name, Place Pigneau de Béhaine. However, this statue was brought down in October 1945, leaving behind only an empty pedestal in the center of the garden. It was not until 1959 that a new statue, that of Our Lady of Peace, was installed to replace the earlier monument. In May 1964, the South Vietnamese government renamed it President John F. Kennedy Square honoring the same name assassinated U.S. President.

Directions: Head east for about a minute or two, and you'll find the Post Office waiting for you. Enjoy the stroll! It is about a minute's walk away.

Stop 2: Post Office

Coordinates: 10.780000, 106.700000

Type/Specialty: Historic Postal Service

Specific Examples: Intricate interior design, vintage postal service artifacts, large wooden counters

The Saigon Central Post Office was completed between 1886 and 1891, during the period when Vietnam was part of French Indochina. The building was designed by Alfred Foulhoux, whose name appears clearly in colonial architectural records, not by Gustave Eiffel as many believe. Shortly after the post office’s opening, the journal Architecte constructeur praised Foulhoux’s efficient layout and artistic façade. Inside, you can see soaring iron arches that are both robust and graceful. The cool iron contrasts with the polished wood counters where postal clerks once worked, stamping letters and parcels. Dương Văn Ngộ worked here as the last public letter writer in Vietnam from 1990 to 2021, marking the post office as a bridge between eras.

Directions: From the Post Office, walk east on Công xã Paris, then turn left onto Nguyễn Văn Bình and continue for about 5 minutes. You’ll enjoy the vibrant atmosphere filled with literary enthusiasts. Continue to Book Street.

Stop 3: Book Street

Coordinates: 10.780573, 106.699695

Type/Specialty: Cultural Street

Specific Examples: Outdoor book stalls, cozy reading spots, local author signings

You are standing on Nguyen Van Binh Street, where Book Street stretches for about 100 meters in the center of Ho Chi Minh City. Here, you find numerous book stalls and shops selling a wide variety of printed books across different genres like literature, politics, society, science, and culture. Book Street was established to promote a reading culture and provide a gathering space for book lovers. You can also see book cafes and enjoy cultural activities, as the street regularly hosts events such as book fairs and author signings. One of the entrances to Book Street is from Hai Ba Trung Street, leading you into this narrow, tree-lined area bustling with activity. Book Street On February 1, 1968, during the Tet Offensive, South Vietnamese police chief Lt. Col. Nguyen Ngoc Loan executed a handcuffed Viet Cong prisoner named Nguyen Van Lem on a Saigon street.

Directions: Head southwest for roughly 600 meters, and you’ll find yourself at the Independence Palace. Enjoy the stroll!

Stop 4: Independence Palace

Coordinates: 10.777050, 106.695370

Type/Specialty: Historic Site

Specific Examples: Beautiful gardens, war history exhibits, guided tours

The Independence Palace you see today began to rise in mid-1962, commissioned by President Ngô Đình Diệm to replace the old Norodom Palace, which had suffered serious damage when two dissident South Vietnamese pilots bombed it. The Independence Palace was designed by architect Ngô Viết Thụ and was the presidential palace, home and workplace of the president of the Republic of Vietnam. The palace finally opened on 31 October 1966 under General Nguyễn Văn Thiệu, who made it his home and office. Inside and out, the building’s modernist design reflects a mid-20th-century ambition to forge a new identity amid turmoil. The gardens around you, orderly and green, offer a quiet contrast to the decisive events that unfolded here. As you move on, a nearby museum preserves the memories of conflict and reconciliation, holding stories that continue to ripple through this city. It was also the site of the Fall of Saigon on 30 April 1975 that ended the Vietnam War, when a Liberation Army of South Vietnam tank crashed through its gates.

Directions: Head northwest for roughly 500 meters, and you'll arrive at the War Remnants Museum. Enjoy your stroll!

Stop 5: War Remnants Museum

Coordinates: 10.779500, 106.692000

Type/Specialty: Museum

Specific Examples: Photographic exhibits, military artifacts, historical documents

Beyond the gate, the museum’s grounds display military aircraft and tanks, their metal bodies bearing the scars of time as mute sentinels. The museum opened on 4 September 1975 under the name Exhibition House for U.S. and Puppet Crimes. The displays trace the arc from the First Indochina War through the Vietnam War, immersing visitors in decades of conflict. The War Remnants Museum is a war museum at 28 Võ Văn Tần Street, Xuân Hòa, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam.

Directions: Head east for about 1.2 kilometers, and you'll reach the stunning Opera House. Enjoy the stroll!

Stop 6: Opera House

Coordinates: 10.776390, 106.702780

Type/Specialty: Cultural Venue

Specific Examples: Stunning facade, ballet and opera performances, guided tours

The Saigon Opera House was designed by French architect Félix Olivier and completed on January 1, 1900, making it a rare surviving example of French colonial architecture in Vietnam. Its façade recalls the Petit Palais in Paris, with flamboyant, intricate reliefs and inscriptions that once drew criticism for being overly ornate. Earlier in its timeline, the Opera House suffered damage during the Allied air raids of 1944 amid World War II, but was restored in 1955 to serve as the seat of South Vietnam’s Lower House. As the legislature later split into two chambers, the building hosted both the Lower House and the Senate, embedding it deep within the political life of the era. The Provisional Revolutionary Government eventually began using the theatre for the People's Assembly, marking a dramatic shift from colonial entertainment to the center of revolutionary governance.

Directions: Head west for roughly 200 meters, and you'll arrive at City Hall. Enjoy the stroll! Continue to City Hall

Stop 7: City Hall
Coordinates: 10.776470, 106.700970
Type/Specialty: Government Building
Specific Examples: Imposing architecture, historical significance, illuminated at night The building before you was designed by architect Fernand Gardè and completed in 1908, opening the following year in 1909.

Its construction marked a decade-long effort beginning in 1898 to create a seat for municipal governance under French colonial rule. The grand opening in 1909 was timed to celebrate 50 years of French presence in Saigon. French Indochina governors-general gathered for the event, using the building as a tangible mark of their influence over the city. Sculptures on the facade, including figures of Marianne—the personification of liberty, equality, and fraternity—stand as reminders of the era’s political imagery. On April 29 and 30, 2023, the building opened its doors to the public for the first time during Reunification Day celebrations.
Directions: Head southeast for roughly 400 meters, and you'll find yourself at Café Apartments 42. Enjoy your stroll!

Stop 8: Café Apartments 42

Coordinates: 10.774089, 106.704056

Type/Specialty: Coffee shop

You are standing in front of the Café Apartment at 42 Nguyễn Huệ in Ho Chi Minh City. Now, it has been transformed into a lively complex of independent cafés. Inside, you find a variety of charming cafes, boutique stores, and restaurants. The building is located on Nguyễn Huệ walking street in District 1.

Directions: Head east for roughly 350 meters, and you'll arrive at Bạch Đằng Pier. Enjoy the stroll!

Stop 9: Bạch Đằng Pier

Coordinates: 10.775240, 106.707002

Type/Specialty: Waterfront

Specific Examples: Scenic river views, boat tours, evening lights

The connection supported commerce and communication in the growing metropolis by threading together the city’s expanding neighborhoods. Today, the water’s surface reflects the city skyline, while the park’s pathways curve through grassy expanses forming lotus shapes, a design completed in 2022 after a major renovation. In the distance, you can see the site of the former Ba Son Shipyard, once a hub of naval activity that has since relocated. The pier’s long-standing role in transport and connection reflects the city’s layered urban fabric, where waterways and roads meet and the river remains a steady axis around which the city turns.

Directions: Head southwest for roughly 1.7 kilometers, and you'll arrive at Thi Bar. Enjoy the stroll!

Stop 10: Thi Bar

Coordinates: 10.767660, 106.693960

Type/Specialty: Gay bar

You are standing outside Thi Bar, located at 224 Đề Thám Street in the Phạm Ngũ Lão area of Ho Chi Minh City. Thi Bar On April 30, 1975, victorious North Vietnamese soldiers raised communist flags outside the Independence Palace, marking the surrender of South Vietnam and the end of the war. This bar has been open since 2010 and welcomes everyone. Live music starts here every night from 10pm, featuring local bands that cover popular songs. The staff are friendly and you can even request your favorite song. Thi Bar is one of the few real gay bars in the city and has outdoor seating. It is closed on Tuesdays, except on holidays when it remains open. Food options inside are limited, so you might want to eat before coming or ask if you can bring outside food.

From Cathedral, Opera House and Thi Bar, this route is the one you chose through the city — your own path, in your own order. That's 10 stops in all.
